name: Vassar Tan
lede: Vassar Tan is a warm orange-brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, close enough to [[polished-brown]] that the two sit side by side in our archive.

sections.title: A 1925 brown
sections.body: Maerz and Paul record Vassar Tan in their 1930 dictionary as first appearing in 1925, on plate 6, chip A11 [1]. The ISCC-NBS revision of 1955 files the same chip under block 55, described as "strong brown" [1]. Our library's nearest named neighbor is [[polished-brown]], a touch darker and less orange; [[sienna]] and [[russet]] sit close behind it [2]. A fourth close match, [[fuzzy-wuzzy]], sits between the two [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Vassar Tan in 1,442 of 23,781 paintings, about 6.1 percent, more common than 89 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1500s, in 139 of 2,231 paintings, 2.3 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent rather than a dominant tone, in 71 percent of its appearances [3]. George Catlin used it most: it appears in 8 of his 50 paintings here, 3.1 times his peers' rate [3]. The earliest match in the archive dates to 1119, eight centuries before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, which only shows a similar hue surviving in an old, varnished canvas, not the pigment or the name itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
